title: 1974: Rudy Wiedoeft and Pee Wee Eisenheimer at Venice
summary: Howard says he asked saxophonist Rudy Wiedoeft at Venice pier to let him play; there was no union then.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, what about -- if I may ask a question now.
Sure.
When did you hear your first jazz?
Oh, well, you're they weren't interested in jazz.
Well, not all the way, but there must have been some point where you heard some jazz players that
Well, I told you where I heard them.
Yeah, but you also heard others that came to be big names in the business and things like that, right?
Oh, yeah, after that Rudy Weidoff.
Did you meet Rudy?
Oh, yeah.
That's what I mean. See, some of those names --
I used to play with him.
How did you meet Rudy? Where did you hear about him?
I heard about him down at the beach. He was down at the beach, so I went down there.
Was that in like Ohio someplace?
No, right here.
Oh, California, huh?
California.
Okay. Like in the Santa Monica area?
No. Down at -- yeah, Santa Monica -- it wasn't Santa Monica. In Venice.
In Venice.
Yeah, right.
Playing on a pier there?
On the pier.
Rudy Weedoff. Do you know about what year that was?
No, I don't know what year that was.
In the '30s?
Huh?
Was it in the '30s?
The '30s? It's a little difficult for me to say.
Okay. But a few years ago, quite a few years ago.
Yeah, quite a few years.
What was he like? What kind of -- I heard records by him. I never got a chance to hear him.
What kind of fellow was he like?
Yeah. I mean was he --
A very, very nice man.
A very musical guy.
A very musical guy. A nice man.
Uh-huh.
He was quite a gentleman, and there's another fellow, Pee Wee Eisenheimer. He's around here now.
Is Pee Wee a saxophone player or what?
Yeah. I see him at the union.
(Laughter)
I guess he's around 80, 81, 82 years old.
Was he working with Rudy?
No, he was just playing different places, they all played, you know. And they played mostly solos. They wasn't playing in a big band.
Well, Rudy Wiedoff has all those -- you know, for years all those books of solos out. Did he play a lot of those too?
Yeah. Oh, yes.
That was kind of the thing in that period, playing those types of songs.
Playing those types of things. And you know who's got -- Pee Wee Eisenheimer. He's around the union now. I see him all the time.
Uh-huh. He was one of those good saxophone players, too?
Oh, yeah. Pee Wee Eisenheimer. I can get you his name out of the book.
Well, we can find that. (Inaudible). we can call too and talk to him.
Boy, he was a fine player.
So what kind of music were they playing at the time. Would that be like Dixieland, or --
Oh, no, no, no.
Swing, or what?
They didn't call it swing then. They
Uh-huh. Ragtime.
Yeah, they didn't call it swing.
With a regular group, like four or five saxes and --
Oh, no, no. They'd have maybe a saxophone a trumpet and a trombone.
Just maybe six or seven pieces.
Six or seven pieces. Didn't have much.
Uh-huh. Were you working with the band at any point, or you just knew him?
Just knew him, and I asked -- you know, asked him to let me play with them.
What was the --
And there wasn't no union here, so you could play like you pleased.
